sounds.intro: Lithuanian is a Baltic language, one of the oldest living Indo-European languages, closely related to Latvian. It uses the Latin alphabet with extra marks. Vowels with a hook (ą, ę, į, ų) or a bar (ū) are long. The dot over ė also makes a long, closed "e". Stress can fall on any syllable and moves between forms of the same word.
rows: long, closed "e", like the "ay" in "say" without the glide
a glide: "ie" like "ye" in "yet" and "uo" like "wo" in "word"
notes: Lithuanian has seven cases and no articles. The words change their endings to show their job in the sentence.
Marks on vowels (accents) show stress in dictionaries but are not written in normal text. The "say" line shows the usual stress. The pool is unreviewed and a few rare words are best guesses.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Lithuanian has "tu" (you, informal) and "jūs" (you, formal or plural). Verbs change for each person. "Jis" is he and "ji" is she, and the plural splits too: "jie" (men) and "jos" (women).

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Lithuanian has no "the" or "a". Masculine nouns end in -as, -is, -ys, -us; feminine in -a, -ė. Plural masculine: -ai, -iai, -ys: knyga, knygos; vaikas, vaikai.

grammar.title: To be: būti
text: The verb "būti" (to be) changes for each person: esu, esi, yra. "Yra" is also used for "there is".

grammar.title: Having: turėti
text: Lithuanian uses "turėti" (to have): turiu mašiną (I have a car). For "I do not have", use "neturiu". "There is no" is "nėra" and takes the genitive.

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Verbs change for person. Regular verbs (like "valgyti", to eat) take -u, -i, -a / -o: aš valgau, tu valgai, jis valgo.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The usual order is subject, verb, object: "aš skaitau knygą" (I read a book). The object ends change: knyga becomes knygą.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "ne" in front of the verb: nežinau (I do not know). With "būti", "nėra" replaces "yra": nėra vandens (there is no water). Nouns after "nėra" take the genitive.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Put "ar" at the start to turn a sentence into a yes / no question: Ar tu esi studentas? (Are you a student?). Answer "taip" (yes) or "ne" (no).

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words come at the start of the sentence.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: Lithuanian possessives do not change: mano (my), tavo (your), jo (his), jos (her), mūsų (our), jūsų (your, formal), jų (their). "Patikti" means "to please": man patinka arbata (tea pleases me).

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Use "jūs" (with "esate", "galite") for one older person, a stranger or in a formal setting. Use "tu" with friends, family and children.

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: past forms (aš valgiau, I ate). Future: end in -siu (aš valgysiu, I will eat). The past of "būti": buvau, buvai, buvo.

grammar.title: Commands
text: Use the "tu" form: eik! (go!), ateik! (come!). Add "-ite" for "jūs": eikite! For "do not", put "ne" before: neik!

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: "Galėti" (can), "turėti" (must) and "norėti" (want) change for person. They are followed by the "to" form of the verb: aš galiu plaukti (I can swim).
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Prepositions: "ant" (on), "po" (under), "šalia" (next to), "prie" (at, by), "netoli" (near). For "in" Lithuanian changes the noun ending: mokykla becomes mokykloje (at school), namai becomes namuose (at home).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add "-esnis / -esnė" to an adjective for "more": didelis, didesnis (big, bigger). For "the most", add "-iausias": didžiausias. "Už" means "than".
